name: Suriname
summary:
Suriname, officially the Republic of Suriname, is a country in northern South America with a population of approximately 600,000 — the smallest sovereign state on the South American continent. Over 90% of its territory is covered by tropical rainforest, the highest proportion of any country in the world. Situated slightly north of the equator, it is bordered by Guyana to the west, French Guiana to the east, Brazil to the south, and the Atlantic Ocean to the north.

Suriname's extraordinary ethnic diversity reflects its colonial history as a plantation colony. Dutch colonization (from 1667) established sugar, coffee, and cocoa plantations worked by enslaved Africans; after abolition (1863), indentured laborers were brought from India, Java (Indonesia), and China. Today Suriname's population is roughly 27% Hindustani (South Asian), 22% Maroon (descendants of escaped African slaves), 16% Creole, 14% Javanese, and 13% Mixed — making it one of the most ethnically diverse nations on earth.

The Maroon communities — descendants of enslaved Africans who escaped Dutch plantations and built free societies in the interior rainforest — are Suriname's most historically remarkable cultural heritage. Six Maroon nations (Saramaka, Ndyuka, Matawai, Aluku, Kwinti, Paamaka) maintain distinct languages, governance structures, and cultural traditions rooted in African heritage. Suriname gained independence from the Netherlands in 1975, though close economic ties and Dutch language use continue. The country is a major bauxite and gold exporter.
